pr_body:
This is an alternative fix for the collision import options, and colliders not showing up when selecting 'Mesh + Static Collider' mentioned in #49752 (it does not however fix the rigid body scaling issue since that seems to be a limitation of the physics engine itself, not the importer). It also fixes the -col and -rigid suffixes mentioned #48945. Although it's mentioned that this might be deprecated, as it stands, the functionality is still intact (it works with -colonly for example), it was simply broken due to using _gen_shape_list rather than _pre_gen_shape_list. Even if it's to be deprecated, it may at least be worth fixing for now since, as pointed out, the usability of setting up collision with the new import menu is still lacking somewhat.

*Bugsquad edit:* Fixes #49752. Fixes #48945.

issue_context.title: New 3D import: GLTF importer creates no collision for -col objects
issue_context.body:
Here's a source .blend file:
[Village.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/6525359/Village.zip)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/491704/119204906-06b0a500-ba97-11eb-85e8-597c72924427.png)
Note the texture mapping and the fact that meshes do have `-col` attribute in their names.

This is how Godot 3.3.1 imports a resulting GLTF file:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/491704/119205787-8fc8db80-ba99-11eb-80ae-01f6fb1a0693.png)

Godot 4 does not create any collision nodes:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/491704/119205857-c0107a00-ba99-11eb-8968-6e621ea3e2c1.png)
comments: As far as I know, this is intentional because the new 3D import system does not rely on import hints anymore: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1823

It seems that's the case.
the problem is - the current state of the advanced import dialog. does not allow to enable collision for more than one object at time -  for large scenes with many objects this is really bad.

Seems to no longer be an issue in 4.0 release candidates.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/39946030/220891610-33e526b0-dcf7-401f-b6c1-82c1437ef225.png)

review_comments: What's the point to do `p_node->replace_by(rigid_body)` to then free `p_node`, and then assign it `rigid_body`? That's pretty confusing.

In the case of p_node, this will be the root of the object which will by default be a Node3D type. For rigid bodies, we first want to use the replace_by function which will replace the Node3D node with a new RigidBody node. The root of this object now be a rigid body, and according to replace_by, the original node still exists, it's simply been removed from the tree.

The reason we call queue_delete on p_node now is since we have removed the original root node, I believe leaving it will cause a memory leak. This was simply to make it consistent with the behaviour of the other two switch cases which do similar things. We then assign p_node the new rigid body node, which has become the new root. This is because lower in the function, p_node is still consider as part of the function.

One thing I could do though is move the rigid_body->set_transform function above rigid_body->set_name which will make it more consistent with the other two switch cases, and hopefully a little less confusing.

Hm, I thought that `replace_by` would modify `p_node`'s `this`, which is why I was confused that we'd free the modified instance. But indeed it doesn't change `p_node`, it takes its place and sets groups and properties accordingly, but leave `p_node` unchanged (and orphaned).

It's a bit of a weird API IMO, but the importer code makes sense then. Thanks for the explanations :)
